subject: Pathology
summary: A full blood count (FBC) gives a snapshot of red cells, white cells and platelets, helping detect anaemia, infection, inflammation or bone‑marrow disease. It guides diagnosis, monitoring and treatment decisions.

sections.p: An FBC measures haemoglobin, red cell indices, white cell differential, and platelet count, usually via automated haematology analyser.
Interpretation uses reference ranges and clinical context. For anaemia, WHO grades severity by Hb thresholds; for infection, WCC and differential patterns suggest bacterial vs viral.
b: Anaemia: Hb <13 g/dL (men), <12 g/dL (women); severe <7 g/dL

sections.p: Common causes vary by setting. In low‑resource areas, infections dominate, followed by nutritional deficiencies and hemoglobinopathies.
FBC abnormalities appear as laboratory findings; clinical clues include fatigue, pallor, fever, bruising or bleeding.
The FBC is the first test; further workup depends on abnormal results.

t.b: Shows cell morphology; confirms microcytosis, hypochromia, sickle cells, blasts.
Low ferritin indicates iron deficiency; high ferritin suggests inflammation or overload.
High retic indicates haemolysis or recovery; low indicates marrow failure.
Assesses bleeding risk when platelets are low.
Used when blasts >5% or unexplained cytopenia.
Screening in all patients with unexplained cytopenia or infection.

sections.p: Severe cytopenias or sudden changes can herald life‑threatening conditions.
b: Marked eosinophilia (>1.5 × 10⁹/L) – parasitic infection or hypereosinophilic syndrome

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, support blood counts, and monitor for complications.
b: Drug‑induced: stop offending agent, supportive care

sections.p: Repeat FBCs to assess response; preventive measures target modifiable risks.
b: Regular monitoring in chronic diseases (e.g., sickle cell)

sections.p: Other tests can mimic FBC findings; awareness prevents misdiagnosis.
b: Complete metabolic panel – may show anaemia of chronic disease but not cause

sections.p: Certain conditions alter FBC interpretation; clinicians must consider context.
b: Platelet clumping in EDTA tubes can falsely lower platelet count

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anaemia with chest pain or dyspnea
Sudden drop in any cell line with symptoms

faq.q: What is the normal range for haemoglobin?
faq.a: ~13.5–17.5 g/dL in men, 12–15.5 g/dL in women.

faq.q: Why is a high eosinophil count important?
faq.a: It suggests parasitic infection, allergic disease or hypereosinophilic syndrome.

faq.q: Can an FBC be normal in infection?
faq.a: Yes, early infection may show normal counts; repeat testing or other markers (CRP, procalcitonin) help.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with fatigue and pallor. Her FBC shows Hb 9 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, ferritin 10 ng/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis and first step in management?
A 45‑year‑old man with fever has WCC 18 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils 85%, platelets 80 × 10⁹/L. What red flag should prompt urgent referral?
A child in a malaria‑endemic area has Hb 8 g/dL, MCV 80 fL, and a positive malaria smear. What is the appropriate treatment strategy?
